proposals.idea: The vessel bought on Dhanteras is counted into the house the same evening; the compressor bought in March still has no tag.
proposals.scene: A new brass vessel comes home and goes straight onto the kitchen shelf, counted. At the factory, the drill bought in March sits by the door with no tag, no owner and no service date, and the day it goes missing nobody can say who had it.
proposals.reelHook: Counted at home. Uncounted at work.
proposals.reelCaption: On Dhanteras the house buys one vessel and counts it in the same evening. Everyone knows where it sits. At the factory the drill bought in March still has no tag. Nobody owns it, nobody knows its service date, and the day it goes missing the question goes round the floor for a week. Every asset costs money twice: once to buy, once to lose. The assets register gives each one a tag, an owner and an audit date, so the count the house does on Dhanteras happens at work every quarter. Save this for the next time something walks off the floor.
proposals.statusLine: The vessel bought today is counted in by tonight. *Is the machine bought in March on any list?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: On Dhanteras my family counts one new vessel into the house before dinner. I have met factories where the compressor bought in March has no tag, no owner and no service date.

proposals.idea: The Dhanteras lamp keeps watch all night while the house sleeps; the reminder desk keeps watch over late work while the owner is at the puja.
proposals.scene: At dusk the lamp is set at the door and kept burning till morning. Across town a quotation promised for Friday has gone quiet, and the only one who notices is the owner, on Sunday, from the client's reply.
proposals.reelHook: One lamp watches the door all night
proposals.reelCaption: On Dhanteras the lamp at the door burns all night so the house can sleep. In most firms the only thing watching late work is the owner, and the owner is at the puja. The quotation promised for Friday goes quiet, nobody chases it, and the client reply on Sunday is the first anyone hears of it. The cost is the order, and the evening. The reminder desk is the lamp at the door: late work gets a WhatsApp nudge, and if it still stalls a coordinator calls the doer and sets a new time. The owner hears only what stayed late after that. Send this to whoever chases for you.
proposals.statusLine: The lamp at the door watches all night. *Who watches the late quotation while you are at the puja?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: The Dhanteras lamp burns at the door all night so the house can sleep. In most firms the only lamp over late work is the owner, and tonight the owner is at the puja.
proposals.carouselCover: *Who watches the door* at work tonight

proposals.idea: The family visits three shops and writes the rate on a slip before buying; the firm pays whoever called last.
proposals.scene: Three jewellers, three rates on a slip, then the choice. At the office the accountant pays the vendor who called twice this morning, and the one who gives sixty days credit, and never calls, is paid first out of habit.
proposals.reelHook: Three shops, one slip, then the choice
proposals.reelCaption: Before anyone buys on Dhanteras the family walks to three shops and writes each rate on a slip. Only then is the choice made. At the office the order of payment is set by who called last. The vendor who called twice this morning is paid today, and the one who matters most waits. The cost is credit you did not need to spend and a supplier you did not need to upset. Vendors and payments writes the order down: who to pay, how much, and in what sequence as cash comes in, decided once, not at every call. Save this for the next payment day.
proposals.statusLine: Three shops before the choice at home. *At work, the vendor who called last gets paid first.*
proposals.linkedinOpening: My family walks to three shops on Dhanteras and writes every rate on a slip before buying. At most firms the order of payment is set by whichever vendor called last.
proposals.carouselCover: Three shops at home, *one phone call at work*

proposals.idea: Diwali cleaning empties the drawer nobody opens; the question tray empties the drawer of questions the team has been saving for the owner.
proposals.scene: The top of the cupboard, the drawer behind the door, the pile that waited all year. At work, forty small questions for the owner wait in forty WhatsApp chats, and each one stops a job until the owner is free.
proposals.reelHook: The drawer nobody opens till Diwali
proposals.reelCaption: Every Diwali the house turns out the drawer nobody opens all year. At work the same drawer is full of questions for the owner. Which rate for this client, which courier, can we give two more days. Forty of them wait in forty chats, and each one stops a job until the owner has a minute. The cost is a floor that waits while the owner is in a meeting. The question tray puts every question in one place, and the owner answers the lot in one sitting, morning and evening. Nothing waits in a chat. Send this to the owner who answers questions at the traffic light.
proposals.statusLine: Diwali cleaning finds the drawer nobody opens. *How many questions are waiting for you in how many chats?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: Diwali cleaning always reaches the drawer nobody opened all year. In most firms that drawer is the forty questions waiting for the owner in forty chats.

proposals.idea: Twenty diyas along the parapet, and the eye goes straight to the one that is out; the owner's screen does that for the whole business.
proposals.scene: The row of diyas lit on the parapet. Nineteen burn and nobody looks at them. The one that has gone out is seen from the road. At work, nineteen jobs are on time and the one that is late is found three days after the client finds it.
proposals.reelHook: Nineteen burn. You see the one.
proposals.reelCaption: Twenty diyas along the parapet on Diwali night. Nineteen burn and nobody looks at them. The eye goes straight to the one that has gone out. That is how an owner should see the business, and it is not how most owners do. Nineteen jobs are on time and the one that is late is discovered three days after the client discovered it, because finding it meant asking nineteen people. The owner's screen puts the whole business on one screen: what is late, what is waiting, who is carrying what. The one that is out is the first thing seen, not the last. Save this for the next Monday morning.
proposals.statusLine: Nineteen diyas burn. The eye finds the one that is out. *Can you find the one late job that fast?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: Twenty diyas on the parapet tonight. Nineteen burn and nobody looks at them. The eye goes straight to the one that has gone out.

proposals.idea: The new account book opens on Diwali night, and the old dues come across with it; the order they are paid in is decided before the first entry.
proposals.scene: The new books marked at Chopda Pujan, the first entry written. The dues from the old year do not vanish with the old book. At work the first week of the new book is spent paying whoever shouts loudest.
proposals.reelHook: A new book. The same old dues.
proposals.reelCaption: On Diwali night the new account book opens and the first entry goes in. The dues from the old book do not vanish with it. They come across, and the first week of the new year is spent paying whoever calls loudest. The cost is cash that goes out in the wrong order and a vendor who mattered left waiting. Vendors and payments sets the order before the first entry: who to pay, how much, and in what sequence as cash comes in. The new book then starts clean in the way that counts, with the order decided once, not at every call. Save this for the week after Diwali.
proposals.statusLine: The new book opens tonight. *Is the order of the old dues written anywhere?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: The new account book opens on Diwali night with one clean entry. The old dues come across with it, and in most firms the order they are paid in is decided by who calls first.

proposals.idea: The year-end count touches every shelf once in a week of clipboards; the stock colour sheet gives the same answer every evening in ten minutes.
proposals.scene: The last week of December, shutters half down, clipboards on every shelf. Three days later the count is known, and it is already wrong, because the first week of January sells what the count said was plenty.
proposals.reelHook: Three days to learn one number
proposals.reelCaption: The last week of December is the stock count. Shutters half down, clipboards on every shelf, three days to learn one number. By the second week of January it is wrong again, and the thing that ran out was the one the count said was plenty. The cost is three days of the floor and a lost order in January. The stock colour sheet gives each product a maximum, and every evening the closing stock gets a colour: buy, hold or sell. The count becomes a ten-minute habit at closing, and the year-end is a check, not a discovery. Save this for the next time a shelf surprises you.
proposals.statusLine: Three days of clipboards for one number. *What colour is your stock tonight?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: The last week of December is clipboards on every shelf and three days to learn one number. By the second week of January that number is already wrong.

proposals.idea: Half the names on the December roster are crossed out; the work they left behind has no name on it at all.
proposals.scene: The leave roster on the wall with half the floor crossed out for the last fortnight. The dispatch that was Ramesh's, the follow-up that was Priya's, now belong to nobody, and the owner finds out which ones on the 2nd of January.
proposals.reelHook: Half the floor on leave. Whose job now?
proposals.reelCaption: The December leave roster has half the names crossed out for the last fortnight. The names are crossed out. The work is not. The dispatch that was one person and the follow-up that was another now belong to nobody, and the owner finds out which ones went quiet on the second of January, from the client. The cost is a fortnight of work with no owner. My Day gives each person one screen: today routines, the steps due and the tasks given to them. When a name goes on leave the steps move to the one covering, and the screen shows them that morning. Send this to whoever is making the roster.
proposals.statusLine: Half the names are crossed off the December roster. *Whose screen does their work appear on tomorrow?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: Half the names on the December roster are crossed out for the last fortnight. The names are crossed out. The work is not.

proposals.idea: The cake was ordered in November and collected on the 24th because the slip was in the drawer; the referral partner who sent two clients in March has not heard from the firm since.
proposals.scene: A bakery slip from November, kept in the drawer, collected on the 24th without a thought. At work the architect who referred two clients in March was thanked once and has not had a call since, and the next referral went to someone who did call.
proposals.reelHook: Ordered in November. Collected on the 24th.
proposals.reelCaption: The cake was ordered in November and collected on the 24th without a thought, because the slip was in the drawer and the date was on it. The architect who referred two clients in March was thanked once and has not heard from the firm since. The next referral went to the one who called in June. The cost is the client you never heard about. Partner follow-up keeps referral partners in tiers, each with a monthly touchpoint that comes up by itself, so the call that keeps a partner happens like the cake: ordered once, collected on the day. Save this before the year-end calls.
proposals.statusLine: The cake slip from November was in the drawer. *When did your referral partner last hear from you?*
proposals.linkedinOpening: The cake was ordered in November and collected on the 24th because the slip was in the drawer. The architect who sent us two clients in March has had no call since.
